Arizona law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there.

What the official sources say

  • An action to recover land from a person in peaceable and adverse possession, cultivating, using and enjoying it, must be commenced within ten years after the cause of action accrues; the possession covers no more than 160 acres (or the enclosed acreage if less), unless held under a recorded written memorandum of title fixing boundaries. (A.R.S. 12-526; source)
  • An action to recover real property from a person in peaceable and adverse possession under title or color of title must be commenced within three years; 'color of title' means a consecutive chain of transfer down to the possessor that is irregular (for example an unrecorded or only written link) but without want of intrinsic fairness and honesty. (A.R.S. 12-523; source)
  • A person is guilty of forcible entry and detainer if he enters real property except where entry is given by law, enters by force, or wilfully and without force holds over after the term ends and after demand for possession by the person entitled. (A.R.S. 12-1171; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Arizona statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • Security deposit plus prepaid rent may not exceed one and one-half month's rent (tenant may voluntarily prepay more). (A.R.S. 33-1321; source)
  • Within 14 days (excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays) after termination, delivery of possession and tenant demand, landlord must provide an itemized list of deductions and amount due; if landlord fails to comply, tenant may recover the money plus damages of twice the amount wrongfully withheld. (A.R.S. 33-1321; source)
  • The holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at termination of tenancy is bound by the security deposit section (relevant on sale). (A.R.S. 33-1321; source)
  • Month-to-month tenancy ends by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date; week-to-week requires at least ten days. (A.R.S. 33-1375(A)-(B); source)
  • Landlord entry: at least two days' notice, at reasonable times; no notice needed in emergency; a tenant's maintenance request waives separate access notice. (A.R.S. 33-1343; source)
  • Landlord must comply with building codes affecting health and safety, make all repairs to keep premises fit and habitable, keep common areas clean and safe, and maintain electrical, plumbing, heating and cooling facilities supplied. (A.R.S. 33-1324(A); source)
  • Retaliation: landlord may not raise rent, decrease services, or bring or threaten an action for possession after the tenant complains to a code enforcement agency, complains to the landlord of a 33-1324 violation, or joins a tenants' union; a complaint within six months before the act creates a presumption of retaliation; exceptions for tenant-caused violations and rent default. (A.R.S. 33-1381; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Arizona law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason.

What the official sources say

  • Nonpayment: if tenant fails to pay within five days after written notice of nonpayment and the landlord's intention to terminate, landlord may terminate by filing a special detainer action. (A.R.S. 33-1368(B)... (nonpayment paragraph); source)
  • Material noncompliance with lease (including material falsification of rental application): written notice, terminates not less than ten days after receipt if not remedied in ten days. (A.R.S. 33-1368; source)
  • Health-and-safety noncompliance by tenant (33-1341): five days' notice; material and irreparable breach on the premises (e.g., weapon discharge, controlled substances, assault, serious property damage): written notice for immediate termination under 33-1377. (A.R.S. 33-1368; source)
  • No-cause end of month-to-month: written notice at least 30 days before the rental date; holdover after term or termination allows an action for possession and, if willful, up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. (A.R.S. 33-1375; source)
  • Special detainer: summons returnable not more than six nor less than three days from issuance; on judgment for plaintiff, court gives judgment for restitution of premises, late charges, costs and (at plaintiff's option) rent due, and grants a writ of restitution; for a material and irreparable breach the trial is no later than the third day after filing and restitution is ordered 12 to 24 hours later. (A.R.S. 33-1377; source)
  • Trial postponement for good cause is at most three days in justice court or five days in superior court (indicating justice court and superior court hear these actions). (A.R.S. 33-1377; source)
